newsitem.title: USA: Home sales jump sharply in February.
newsitem.headline: Home sales jump sharply in February.

text.p: Sales of previously owned homes soared last month to the second-highest level on record as relatively low interest rates and a strong economy kept buyers in the market, a real estate trade group said Thursday.

The National Association of Realtors said that sales of existing, or previously occupied, homes rose 9.0 percent in February to a seasonably adjusted annual rate of 4.26 million units from a revised 3.91 million units in January.
Wall Street economists had forecast February sales of 4.05 million units.
The February sales rate was up 5.2 percent from sales of 4.05 million in February last year and reached its highest level since May 1996's record-setting 4.28 million units.

The median price of an existing home rose fell to $117,500 in February from $120,600 in January, but it rose from the year-ago price of $114,000. The supply of homes rose to 6.2 months' worth from 5.9 months worth in January.
The group's chief economist said he does not expect the Federal Reserve's recent decision to raise interest rates to cause a "notable decline" in home sales.
"The increase in mortgage rates won't be high enough to pull people out of the market or cause them to postpone purchasing decisions," NAR Chief Economist John Tuccillo said.
But at a news conference following the release of the report, Tuccillo said he still expects activity to level off some. "The housing market will be down over the next few months," he said.
Mortgage rates for a 30-year loan averaged 7.65 percent in February, down from 7.82 percent in January but up from 7.08 percent in February a year ago.
A regional breakdown showed the West posting the strongest sales performance, with a rate of 1.0 million units, a gain of 13.6 percent from the month earlier.

In the South, homes sales rose 5.5 percent to 1.53 million units in February. In the Midwest, the February rate of 1.1 million units was up 10 percent from the month before. The Northeast rate rose 8.6 percent to 630,000.
